'''Marvin Isadore Knopp''' (January 4, 1933 – December 24, 2011) was an American [[mathematician]] who worked primarily in [[number theory]]. He made
notable contributions to the theory of [[modular form]]s.

== Life and education ==
Knopp was born on January 4, 1933, in [[Chicago, Illinois]]. He received his [[PhD]] under [[Paul T. Bateman]] from the [[University of Illinois]] in 1958 where he became friends with fellow student [[Gene Golub]].<ref name="golub-mem-vid">{{cite web|url=http://icme.stanford.edu/history/golub_celebration_2008/videos.php |title=Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering - Videos of Speakers at the Gene Golub Remembrance |access-date=2011-12-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105193335/http://icme.stanford.edu/history/golub_celebration_2008/videos.php |archive-date=2011-11-05 }}, Video of Knopp's Talk at Gene Golub Memorial (Talk #3), retrieved 2011-12-29.</ref>
Over the course of his career, he advised twenty Ph.D. students.<ref name="meth-genealogy">[https://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=3978], Knopp's Math Genealogy Entry, retrieved 2011-12-29.</ref> He is the father of pianist Seth Knopp, and of Yehudah, Abby, and Elana.<ref name="memorial-blog">[https://marvinknopp.blogspot.com/], Marvin Knopp Tribute Blog, retrieved 2012-01-09.</ref> Marvin was married to Josephine Zadovsky Knopp for 25 years. Knopp died on December 24, 2011, during a vacation in Florida with his partner of 30 years and common law wife Phyllis Zemble. Marvin found happiness from his children, old movies, great music and numbers. During the 6 years following his death, his papers and books were organized (with the help of Wladimer Pribitkin), his photographs and his mathematical correspondence, were donated to the [[American Institute of Mathematics]] (AIM). On AIM's website, you can find 131 of [https://aimath.org/cgi-bin/library.cgi?database=reprints;mode=display;BrowseTitle=Knopp,%20Marvin Knopp's reprints].

== Personal life ==
Knopp was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]] in 1933. He was an [[Ashkenazi Jews|Ashkenazi Jew]].{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

== Career ==
After receiving his [[PhD]] in 1958, Knopp taught at the [[University of Wisconsin]] and then, for a few years, at the
[[University of Illinois Chicago]] before moving, in 1976, to [[Temple University]] where he stayed until his sudden death in 2011.<ref name="tugeo">{{cite web|url=http://templegeom.org/2011/12/26/marvin-knopp-%D7%96%D7%B4%D7%9C/ |title=Marvin Knopp, ז״ל &#124; Temple Geometry Group |access-date=2011-12-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426081608/http://templegeom.org/2011/12/26/marvin-knopp-%D7%96%D7%B4%D7%9C/ |archive-date=2012-04-26 }}, Temple University Geometry Blog, retrieved 2011-12-29.</ref>
Knopp was a leading expert in the theory of modular forms and a pioneering figure in the theory of [https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Eichler_cohomology Eichler cohomology], modular integrals and generalized modular forms. He was closely associated with [[Emil Grosswald]].<ref name="uiuc-newsletter">[http://www.math.uiuc.edu/mathtimes/MathTimesSP91.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150419183930/http://www.math.uiuc.edu/mathtimes/MathTimesSP91.pdf|date=2015-04-19}}, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Mathematics Newsletter Spring 1991, retrieved 2011-12-29.</ref> In [[Jean Dieudonné]]'s influential book ''A Panorama of Pure Mathematics'' ([[Academic Press]], 1982),
he is mentioned (p.&nbsp;95) as one of those who "made substantial contributions" to the theory of modular forms.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A panorama of pure mathematics (as seen by N. Bourbaki) by Jean Dieudonné - PDF Drive |url=http://www.pdfdrive.com/a-panorama-of-pure-mathematics-as-seen-by-n-bourbaki-e165717161.html |access-date=2022-12-03 |website=www.pdfdrive.com}}</ref>
